boundary_rationale: This row opens the book’s third-person frame with the superscription “The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem:” (web:Eccl.1.1). The verse leads with the construct דִּבְרֵי֙ קֹהֶ֣לֶת (oshb:Eccl.1.1, byte tier), the sole superscription among four verse-initial ḏivrei sites in the book — the other three sit mid-discourse as genitive phrases rather than headers (sweep: 4 verses). The royal formula בֶּן דָּוִ֔ד מֶ֖לֶךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם (oshb:Eccl.1.1, byte tier) supplies the frame’s own king-identification, distinct in voice from the monologue’s later first-person self-identification.

device_notes: This frame verse carries no hevel token and no tachat-hashemesh formula; both begin once the monologue proper opens.

boundary_rationale: The motto stands as its own third-person frame intrusion: “Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher; “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” (web:Eccl.1.2). הֲבֵ֤ל הֲבָלִים֙ ... הֲבֵ֥ל הֲבָלִ֖ים הַכֹּ֥ל הָֽבֶל (oshb:Eccl.1.2, byte tier) carries the superlative doubling twice in one verse, framed by the said-qohelet formula אָמַ֣ר קֹהֶ֔לֶת (oshb:Eccl.1.2, byte tier) — one of three amar-qohelet third-person intrusions in the book (sweep: 3 verses). This inclusio-opening verse is bracketed at the monologue’s far end by its own plene-definite counterpart, a recurrence this row does not itself argue since that verse lies well outside its span.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 1:2 as the opening line of the nature poem rather than a separate frame unit was considered and rejected: the said-qohelet formula marks it as reported third-person speech, a register the poem does not otherwise use.

device_notes: Deviation disclosure: this row keeps frame_narration for a verse some readings treat as the poem’s opening line; the said-qohelet formula and third-person verb argue for frame status over wisdom_poem here.

boundary_rationale: The prologue poem runs as one sustained argument from its governing question to its closing verdict, with no first-person marker or vocative restart anywhere inside it to cut it apart. It opens מַה יִּתְר֖וֹן (oshb:Eccl.1.3, byte tier) — “What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?” (web:Eccl.1.3) — then illustrates the question with four recurring-cycle images (sun, wind, rivers, generations) before turning gnomic at 1:8’1:10, closing אֵ֥ין זִכְר֖וֹן לָרִאשֹׁנִ֑ים (oshb:Eccl.1.11, byte tier), “There is no memory of the former…” (web:Eccl.1.11). This closing verdict on memory coincides with a petuchah (single-witness, tier-3 corroboration) in the Masoretic paragraphing at oshb:Eccl.1.11.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Eccl.1.11 (petuchah, single-witness, tier-3 corroboration of the poem's close)

boundary_rationale: A second shavti turn opens the row, וְשַׁ֧בְתִּי אֲנִ֛י וָאֶרְאֶ֥ה (oshb:Eccl.4.7, byte tier) — “Then I returned and saw vanity under the sun.” (web:Eccl.4.7) — the same resumptive formula that opened 4:1, here introducing the solitary toiler observation of 4:8: “There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother… This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.” (web:Eccl.4.8). MT 4:8 carries a paseq seg (single-witness, count-only) and a ketiv/qere note (the eyes/eye number variant, per the staged pmarks inventory) not engaged by this row’s own boundary argument.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row back to include 4:1-3 was rejected: 4:7 restarts the shavti formula fresh, marking a new observation cycle rather than a continuation of the earlier oppression comparison.

boundary_rationale: A patterned companionship poem answers the solitary toiler of 4:8: טוֹבִ֥ים הַשְּׁנַ֖יִם מִן הָאֶחָ֑ד (oshb:Eccl.4.9, byte tier) — “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.” (web:Eccl.4.9) — develops across three parallel illustrations (falling, warmth, and resistance) before closing, “…and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (web:Eccl.4.12).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping this stretch as monologue_unit (the parent's operative default) was considered and rejected: unlike the surrounding first-person narration, 4:9-12 carries no first-person verb at all and runs a tightly patterned three-fold anaphora ('if...then'), a formal structure closer to the book's other patterned poems than to sustained autobiographical prose.

boundary_rationale: The poor-youth-and-old-king narrative opens on a tov comparative, ט֛וֹב יֶ֥לֶד מִסְכֵּ֖ן וְחָכָ֑ם (oshb:Eccl.4.13, byte tier) — “Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who doesn’t know how to receive admonition any more.” (web:Eccl.4.13) — and develops through the prison-to-throne reversal of 4:14 and the crowd-observation of 4:15 to its closing verdict, כִּֽי גַם זֶ֥ה הֶ֖בֶל וְרַעְי֥וֹן רֽוּחַ (oshb:Eccl.4.16, byte tier), “…Surely this also is vanity and a chasing after wind.” (web:Eccl.4.16). The referents of “the youth, the other, who succeeded him” (web:Eccl.4.15) are not named in the row’s own bytes, and this writer holds the identification of the two figures as genuinely open rather than resolving it by conjecture.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the narrative at 4:14 (the prison-to-throne reversal) from 4:15-16 (the crowd observation) was considered; it was rejected because no first-person or discourse-restart marker separates them, and the closing verdict at 4:16 depends grammatically on the same narrated succession the whole unit describes.
